name: Tower Villa
description: An asymmetrical block with a tower at the inside angle of an L, the entrance at the tower's foot, and the principal rooms opening off a hall that runs from it. The tower is not an ornament added to a plan: it is the plan's pivot. It takes the front door, the stair and the top-floor belvedere, and because it does, the two ranges of the L are freed from having to be symmetrical about anything - which is precisely what the picturesque theorists wanted and what the Georgian plan could not give them. Take the tower away and the diagram collapses into an ordinary side-hall house with an awkward corner. An Italianate tower villa of the largest sort runs to 5,500 sf with a service wing and a conservatory. The range above is what these rooms reach; it was 5,500, of which 97% was reachable (OQ 45).

rooms.name: Entrance Porch
rooms.note: At the foot of the tower, in the angle of the L. Round-arched and usually single-storey against the tower's height, which is what makes the tower read as tall.

rooms.name: Hall
rooms.note: In the tower's base, and it is a hall in the Georgian sense - a room you pass through - rather than the living hall of the Shingle types. The difference matters: this diagram is picturesque in its massing and conventional in its circulation.

rooms.name: Stair
rooms.note: In the tower, rising past a tall arched window on the half-landing that lights it from outside the room - the tower's own reason for existing beyond the view from the top.

rooms.name: Drawing Room
rooms.note: In the front range, with a canted bay to the garden - the bay is the type's second signature after the tower.

rooms.name: Kitchen
rooms.note: In the rear range of the L, which is the wing the tower's asymmetry exists to permit.

scaling.note: Grows by lengthening either arm of the L, which the asymmetry absorbs without strain - this is the type's practical advantage over a symmetrical block and the reason it was popular with builders. What it cannot absorb is a taller neighbour on the plan: the tower must stay the highest thing, and a two-storey wing with a steep roof beside a three-storey tower will read as taller than it and take the composition apart.

trades_away: The whole apparatus of the symmetrical front, and with it the ability to compose a facade to a classical order - the type wears its classicism as brackets, quoins and round-arched openings rather than as proportion. It trades away a compact service route: the L puts the kitchen a long way from the front door, which is why the type always has a back hall. And the tower is expensive per square foot of usable room, since most of its volume is stair.
exemplars: Morse-Libby House (Victoria Mansion), Portland, Maine, Henry Austin, 1858-60
Camden Park, Sydney - the Australian reading of the same diagram
The villas in A. J. Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850), Designs XXIII-XXVIII
Osborne House, Isle of Wight, Prince Albert and Thomas Cubitt, 1845-51 - the royal exemplar the type descends from
sources: A. J. Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850)
editorial: the room list is a composable reduction of the type
